questions.prompt: State the relative electrical charge of a proton.
State the relative electrical charge of a neutron.
questions.answer: 0 (neutral).

questions.prompt: State where most of the mass of an atom is found.
questions.answer: In the nucleus.

title: Atomic number, mass number and isotopes

questions.prompt: Define atomic number.
questions.answer: The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom.

questions.prompt: Define mass number.
questions.answer: The total number of protons and neutrons in an atom.

questions.prompt: Define isotopes.
questions.answer: Atoms of the same element that have different numbers of neutrons.

questions.prompt: State how the number of electrons in a neutral atom compares with the number of protons.
questions.answer: They are equal, so the atom has no overall electrical charge.

questions.prompt: State what an atom becomes if it loses one or more outer electrons.
questions.answer: A positive ion.

questions.prompt: State what happens to an electron in an atom that absorbs electromagnetic radiation.
questions.answer: It moves to a higher energy level, further from the nucleus.

title: Development of the model of the atom

questions.prompt: Describe the plum pudding model of the atom.
questions.answer: A ball of positive charge with negative electrons embedded in it.

questions.prompt: State what the alpha particle scattering experiment showed about the atom.
questions.answer: The mass of the atom is concentrated at the centre (the nucleus), and the nucleus is charged.

questions.prompt: Name the scientist who proposed that electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances.
questions.answer: Niels Bohr.

questions.prompt: Name the three types of nuclear radiation emitted by radioactive nuclei (other than neutrons).
questions.answer: Alpha, beta and gamma.

questions.prompt: State what an alpha particle is made of.
questions.answer: Two neutrons and two protons (a helium nucleus).

questions.prompt: State which of alpha, beta and gamma radiation is the most penetrating.
questions.answer: Gamma.

title: Beta particles, gamma rays and ionising power

questions.prompt: State which type of nuclear radiation has the greatest ionising power.
questions.answer: Alpha.

questions.prompt: Describe what a beta particle is.
questions.answer: A high-speed electron ejected from the nucleus as a neutron turns into a proton.

questions.prompt: State what a gamma ray is.
questions.answer: Electromagnetic radiation emitted from the nucleus.

questions.prompt: Define radioactive decay.
questions.answer: A random process in which an unstable nucleus gives out radiation as it changes to become more stable.

questions.prompt: State the unit of activity.
questions.answer: The becquerel (Bq).

questions.prompt: Define count-rate.
questions.answer: The number of decays recorded each second by a detector.

questions.prompt: State the symbol used for an alpha particle in a nuclear equation.
questions.answer: ⁴₂α (equivalently ⁴₂He).

questions.prompt: State the symbol used for a beta particle in a nuclear equation.
questions.answer: ⁰₋₁β (equivalently ⁰₋₁e).

questions.prompt: State what the emission of a gamma ray does to the mass number and charge of the nucleus.
questions.answer: Neither changes.

questions.prompt: Define half-life.
questions.answer: The time it takes for the number of nuclei of an isotope in a sample to halve, or for the count rate (or activity) to fall to half its initial level.

questions.prompt: State why it is impossible to predict when one particular nucleus will decay.
questions.answer: Radioactive decay is a random process.

questions.prompt: Calculate the number of half-lives needed for a count rate to fall from 800 counts per minute to 100 counts per minute.
Define radioactive contamination.
questions.answer: The unwanted presence of materials containing radioactive atoms on other materials.

questions.prompt: State the difference between contamination and irradiation.
questions.answer: Contamination is unwanted radioactive material on another material; irradiation exposes an object to radiation, and the object does not become radioactive.

questions.prompt: State why the findings of studies into the effects of radiation on humans should be published.
questions.answer: So that other scientists can check them through peer review.

questions.prompt: Name a natural source of background radiation.
questions.answer: Rocks, or cosmic rays from space.

questions.prompt: Name a man-made source of background radiation.
questions.answer: Fallout from nuclear weapons testing or nuclear accidents.

questions.prompt: State what can affect the level of background radiation and radiation dose a person receives.
questions.answer: Occupation and/or location.

questions.prompt: Name a medical use of nuclear radiation for exploring internal organs.
questions.answer: Medical tracers and imaging, e.g. a gamma camera.

questions.prompt: Name a medical use of nuclear radiation for destroying unwanted tissue.
questions.answer: Radiotherapy (treating cancer).

questions.prompt: Explain why alpha emitters are unsuitable as tracers inside the body.
questions.answer: Alpha is strongly ionising with a very short range, so it is absorbed by tissue and cannot be detected from outside the body.

questions.prompt: Define nuclear fission.
questions.answer: The splitting of a large, unstable nucleus (such as uranium or plutonium).

questions.prompt: State what an unstable nucleus usually must do before it undergoes fission.
questions.answer: It must first absorb a neutron.

questions.prompt: State what type of chain reaction causes the explosion of a nuclear weapon.
questions.answer: An uncontrolled chain reaction.

questions.prompt: Define nuclear fusion.
questions.answer: The joining of two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus.

questions.prompt: State what can happen to some of the mass in a fusion reaction.
questions.answer: It may be converted into the energy of radiation.

questions.prompt: Name the process that releases energy in the core of the Sun.
questions.answer: Nuclear fusion.
